questions.q: What question does segregation of duties (SoD) ask, as distinguished from least privilege in this lesson?
options: Can one person, alone, complete an entire sensitive process end to end?
Does this one account have too much access for its job?
How often should passwords be changed?
Which encryption algorithm should protect data at rest?
questions.explain: Least privilege scopes a single account's permissions; SoD asks whether a whole sensitive process can be completed, start to finish, by one person alone.

questions.q: In the accounts payable example, what happens if the same person can create a vendor, approve it, and issue payment?
options: There is no independent check anywhere in the chain, which is a common pattern behind real payment fraud
The process becomes faster with no added risk
SQL Server automatically blocks the transaction
The vendor record is automatically flagged as fraudulent
questions.explain: Without splitting the three functions across different people, nothing stops that person from creating a fake vendor and paying it — committing fraud without needing to collude with anyone.

questions.q: How does this lesson say SoD maps onto the four access-governance roles from Lesson 12?
options: Letting the same person be both requester and approver removes the independent check on that access grant, the same flaw as the vendor-payment example
SoD has no connection to access governance roles
SoD only applies to financial systems, never to access decisions
SoD requires that the auditor also be the provisioner
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct parallel: self-approval of one's own access request is structurally identical to one person controlling an entire payment process.

questions.q: What is a 'toxic combination' as defined in this lesson?
options: A specific pair of permissions or functions that should never be held by the same person
A password that fails complexity requirements
A database table that contains both PII and financial data
Any permission granted without a formal request ticket
questions.explain: Examples given include 'can grant database access' plus 'can approve their own access requests,' and 'can write to the audit log' plus 'no independent review of it.'

questions.q: What does an SoD conflict matrix do?
options: Lists sensitive functions and flags which pairs are toxic when held by the same person
Tracks which servers have the latest security patches installed
Records which users have logged in during the last 24 hours
Calculates the encryption strength of a given algorithm
questions.explain: Running a person's actual entitlements against the conflict matrix — typically as part of an access review — surfaces violations that accumulated without anyone designing them on purpose.
